claim: Chinese Xiaohongshu micro-creators (Key Opinion Consumers) receive only about 35% of the commission a marketer budgets for them, with roughly 55% taken by social and MCN agencies and roughly 10% by the platform.
stance_target: The claim that headline creator pay rates and brand-deal budgets massively overstate creator take-home income because intermediaries capture the majority
scope_conditions: China, Xiaohongshu (RED) platform, KOC tier (5,000-20,000 followers); figure attributed to a single creator informant (Fan, cosmetics vertical) in a 24-person qualitative ethnography, fieldwork Dec 2021-Sep 2023; NOT a survey estimate and NOT Southeast Asia
quoted_support: the platform takes another cut—as Fan revealed, about 10% of the rewards—from marketers' payment to the KOCs ... Hence, KOCs only gain 35% of the commission fee the marketers plan to pay.

claim: Micro-creator compensation is structurally undocumented: marketers merge KOC budget lines into KOL and celebrity lines because KOCs are too cheap to justify the administrative overhead, so their payments never appear as a line item in corporate records.
stance_target: The claim that creator income data is scarce not by accident but because the payment infrastructure is designed not to record small creator payments -- an explanation for why administrative income statistics on creators do not exist
scope_conditions: China, Xiaohongshu influencer-marketing campaigns; based on interviews with marketers and agency associates in a qualitative ethnography; not Southeast Asia
quoted_support: funds allocated for KOCs are merged with those for KOLs and celebrities. This is because, as Celia explained, 'Because KOCs cost only little money.'

claim: Documented quit mechanism: repeated failure to reach engagement thresholds required for brand partnerships leads creators to abandon monetization ambitions entirely, without any formal exit event that platform telemetry would record.
stance_target: The claim that creator attrition is a gradual abandonment of monetization ambition rather than a discrete account-deletion event, so channel-survival telemetry undercounts occupational exit
scope_conditions: China, Xiaohongshu; single informant case (Iris) within a 16-creator interview sample; illustrative not distributional
quoted_support: After several failed attempts to secure partnerships, Iris gave up seeking advertorial opportunities and abandoned her ambitions to become a KOC.

claim: Algorithmic niche lock-in is a documented burnout driver: after six months in a single content vertical, a creator reported exhaustion and believed the algorithm had classified him such that pivoting to other content was infeasible.
stance_target: The claim that platform recommendation systems create switching costs that convert content fatigue into exit rather than pivot
scope_conditions: China, Xiaohongshu; single informant (Jasper) in a 16-creator sample; self-reported perception of algorithm behaviour, not measured
quoted_support: After six months as a 'good-looking' content creator, Jasper grew tired of taking good-looking pictures daily ... 'I think the platform algorithm has labeled me as an aesthetic content creator – it might be hard to change to other areas.'

claim: Successful monetization on Xiaohongshu in this sample was confined to creators with prior professional social-media-marketing experience, leading the authors to conclude that monetization opportunities are inaccessible to most content creators.
stance_target: The claim that creator income is gated by pre-existing professional capital rather than content quality or effort, so median-creator income outcomes are far worse than visible-creator outcomes suggest
scope_conditions: China, Xiaohongshu, 16 creator informants; qualitative inference by the authors, not a measured rate
quoted_support: The seemingly accessible opportunities for personal flourishing through monetizing content are in fact inaccessible to many, if not most, content creators
numbers: 2 named successful monetizers, both with prior marketing careers

claim: Xiaohongshu had over 200 million monthly active users and over 43 million content creators posting by 2022, giving a creator-to-user ratio of roughly 1 in 5 on a single Chinese platform.
stance_target: Establishing the scale of the creator population against which any absolute count of successful creators must be read
scope_conditions: China, Xiaohongshu, 2022; figure cited by the authors from a secondary source, not independently verified; platform-reported
quoted_support: By 2022, RED had over 200 million monthly active users with over 43 million content creators posting on the platform

claim: Chinese content creation absorbs graduate unemployment under an explicit state 'flexible employment' policy, meaning creator population growth there is partly a policy artefact rather than an organic labour-market signal.
stance_target: The claim that creator-population trends are country-specific and driven by local labour-market and policy conditions, so cross-country generalisation of creator growth is invalid
scope_conditions: China, 2022-2023; contextual discourse analysis of state policy and media coverage, not a measured effect on creator entry
quoted_support: Since 2022, amidst a challenging job market in which one in five of the 10.76 million college graduates in China faced unemployment and anxiety about their future, the flexibility provided by platform economy has become particularly attractive.
